title: Did Moses Struggle with Pride?
paragraphs:
Did Moses Struggle with Pride?
The Hidden Battle That Nearly Cost the Humblest Man on Earth Everything
What if one of the greatest men in Scripture wrestled with the very thing most believers refuse to admit still lives inside them?
Not lust.
Not greed.
Not unbelief.
Pride.
The uncomfortable kind.
The subtle kind.
The kind that hides behind good intentions, spiritual success, leadership experience, ministry accomplishments, and years of walking with God.
The kind that can quietly grow in the heart while everyone around you assumes you're holy.
Because if pride could find its way into the life of Moses, it can find its way into ours.
And that realization should stop every one of us in our tracks.
Most Christians know Moses as the great deliverer of Israel.
The man who stood before Pharaoh.
The man through whom God split the Red Sea.
The man who received the Torah on Mount Sinai.
The man who spoke with God "face to face" as a friend speaks with a friend.
Yet Scripture records one shocking moment that still echoes through history.
One moment.
One outburst.
One decision.
And Moses lost the privilege of entering the Promised Land.
That should make every believer lean in.
Because God is not trying to embarrass Moses.
God is warning us.
The story unfolds in Numbers 20.
Israel is once again complaining about water.
After decades of witnessing miracles, the people are still grumbling.
Still accusing.
Still doubting.
Still acting as if God has abandoned them.
Moses and Aaron fall before the Lord.
God gives a clear instruction.
Speak to the rock.
Not strike it.
Speak to it.
The Hebrew text is remarkably direct.

"וְדִבַּרְתֶּם אֶל־הַסֶּלַע"
(ve-dibbartem el-ha-sela)
"Speak to the rock."
Yet Moses does something different.
Standing before the rebellious congregation, he says:

"שִׁמְעוּ־נָא הַמֹּרִים"
(shim'u-na ha-morim)
"Hear now, you rebels."
Then comes the statement that should make every reader pause.

"הֲמִן־הַסֶּלַע הַזֶּה נוֹצִיא לָכֶם מָיִם"
(ha-min ha-sela hazeh notzi lakhem mayim)
"Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?"
Notice the word.
"We."
Not God.
"We."
Then Moses strikes the rock twice.
Water pours out.
The people drink.
The miracle still happens.
But God is not pleased.
In fact, He is angry.
Many readers have wondered why the punishment seems so severe.
After all, Moses was under pressure.
The people were exhausting.
The miracle succeeded.
Water came out.
What was the real issue?
God Himself explains.

"Because you did not trust in Me to uphold Me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel..."
(Numbers 20:12)
The problem was not merely striking the rock.
The deeper issue was that Moses misrepresented God.
For a brief but devastating moment, Moses placed himself at the center of what belonged entirely to the Lord.
Was this pride?
Scripture never explicitly says, "Moses became proud."
But the evidence forces us to ask the question.
The Bible describes Moses as:

"Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all people who were on the face of the earth."
(Numbers 12:3)
The Hebrew word is:

"עָנָו"
(anav)
It describes someone who is lowly before God, dependent upon Him, surrendered to Him.
Yet humility is not something you achieve once and keep forever.
Humility is something you continually choose.
Even the humblest man on earth can stumble if he stops depending on God.
That should both humble and encourage us.
Because many believers assume that maturity removes temptation.
It does not.
Spiritual maturity often changes the form temptation takes.
Young believers may struggle with obvious sins.
Older believers may struggle with invisible ones.
Recognition.
Influence.
Control.
Self-importance.
The need to be right.
The desire for credit.
The temptation to believe God needs them.
And that is where pride becomes most dangerous.
Not when it shouts.
When it whispers.
Moses had spent decades carrying an impossible burden.
Leading difficult people.
Enduring constant criticism.
Interceding for rebels.
Sacrificing comfort.
Bearing responsibility.
Could years of pressure have produced frustration?
Certainly.
Could frustration have opened the door for pride?
Possibly.
Could pride and anger have become intertwined?
Scripture strongly suggests they did.
Because pride often reveals itself when our authority is challenged.
When people do not appreciate us.
When our sacrifices go unnoticed.
When we feel justified in our anger.
The truth is that pride rarely announces itself.
It disguises itself as righteousness.
That is why so many believers fail to recognize it.
The Pharisees were proud and thought they were defending truth.
The older brother in Jesus' parable was proud and thought he was being faithful.
Peter was proud and thought he was being loyal.
Even after walking on water, Peter eventually declared:
"Even if all fall away, I never will."
A few hours later he denied Christ three times.
Pride always overestimates itself.
Humility always depends on God.
The Greek word often associated with humility in the New Testament is:

"ταπεινοφροσύνη"
(tapeinophrosynē)
It literally means lowliness of mind.
Not self-hatred.
Not insecurity.
Not weakness.
It is seeing yourself accurately before God.
Nothing more.
Nothing less.
And that is where Moses' story becomes deeply personal.
Because most of us are not worried about becoming Pharaoh.
We are worried about surviving another week.
Paying bills.
Raising children.
Healing from betrayal.
Fighting temptation.
Leading ministries.
Serving families.
Navigating disappointment.
Yet pride sneaks into ordinary lives every day.
When we refuse correction.
When we need recognition.
When we compare ourselves to others.
When we secretly believe we deserve better.
When we make God's work about our reputation.
When our identity becomes tied to our achievements rather than Christ.
The scandal is not that Moses struggled.
The scandal is that any of us think we are incapable of the same thing.
Yet this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Moses' story does not end in failure.
It ends in grace.
Years after his death, another mountain appears.
Another glorious moment.
Another revelation.
This time it is not Sinai.
It is the Mount of Transfiguration.
And standing beside Jesus is Moses.
The man who failed.
The man who struck the rock.
The man who never entered the earthly Promised Land.
Now standing in glory with the Messiah Himself.
What a picture of redemption.
What a picture of grace.
What a picture of the Gospel.
Failure did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
This is why Christianity is unlike every false religion in the world.
The Bible never hides the failures of its heroes.
Noah got drunk.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Moses failed.
Yet God keeps writing.
Keeps redeeming.
Keeps restoring.
Keeps transforming.
Because our hope is not found in flawless people.
Our hope is found in a flawless Savior.
Even Moses ultimately points beyond himself.
In 1 Corinthians 10, Paul explains that the rock in the wilderness pointed to Christ.
The rock was never the hero.
Moses was never the hero.
Israel was never the hero.
Jesus was always the hero.
The One who would be struck for our sins.
The One who would provide living water.
The One who would satisfy thirsty souls forever.
The One who takes proud rebels and turns them into redeemed children.
Maybe that is why this story still grips us thousands of years later.
Because we recognize ourselves in it.
We know what it feels like to be frustrated.
We know what it feels like to fail.
We know what it feels like to let God down.
We know what it feels like to discover ugly things hiding in our hearts.
But we also know what it feels like to be pursued by grace.
The same grace that restored Peter.
The same grace that transformed Paul.
The same grace that welcomed Moses into glory.
The same grace that still calls your name today.
Maybe pride has been hiding beneath your success.
Maybe beneath your ministry.
Maybe beneath your pain.
Maybe beneath your accomplishments.
Maybe beneath your wounds.
Ask God to reveal it.
Not to condemn you.
To heal you.
Because humility is not thinking less of yourself.
Humility is thinking of Christ more.
And when Christ becomes greater, pride begins to lose its grip.
Be honest.
This probably hit harder than you expected.
The same hand that wrote grace over Moses' failure is still writing over your story.
